figures.caption: Figure 2: Corpus growth over the 14-month collection window aggregated to weekly buckets. (a) Weekly token volume; (b) cumulative volume with a dashed straight-line reference between the first and the last week. Token values are a growth-shape proxy from 224,763 scanned files (partial (97.3% of files)); headline scale claims use the observed log, prompt and storage counts.

Figure 3: Cumulative log count by source population, with a sixmonth linear projection (dotted) fitted on the last 10 weeks of observed data. “Team” refers to the publisher’s internal contributors; “Community” is the union of all externally-attributable named-user sessions. Community dominates team by approximately 24× (156,203 versus 6,286); the projection extends community to ∼242k logs and team to a near-flat ∼ 6.3k logs at week 89 (Nov 2026). The two observed curves sum to 162,489 logs and do not match the corpus headline of 230,935 session logs: the remaining ∼ 68k logs run under root or unidentified filename-usernames (typically internal lab containers, CI runners, automated harnesses and pristine VMs) and are excluded from the named-user attribution rather than redistributed across the two curves.

Figure 8: Credential-leak landscape across the 230,935 cached session pickles. Each bubble is one credential family; x is the number of distinct values observed across the corpus (log scale), y is the number of sessions containing at least one match (log scale), and bubble area is proportional to raw hit count. The numeric tag inside each bubble keys into the legend strip below the axis. Distinct-username counts (u) per family: OpenAI proj. u=112, Anthropic u=19, OpenAI legacy u=17, GitHub PAT u=4, AWS access u=8, Google API u=38, Slack token u=1, JWT u=104, private key u=14. JWTs and OpenAI project keys occupy the top-right “diffuse” quadrant; GitHub PATs and AWS keys sit in the bottom-left “concentrated” quadrant. Counts are entropy-filtered to drop model-hallucinated placeholder shapes (1234567890..., alternating-digit-letter sequences); JWTs and private-key blocks bypass the filter because the structural regex already vouches for them.

Figure 4: Weekly mean user-prompt length (characters) over the 14- month collection window, with a six-month linear projection (dotted) fitted on the last 12 weeks of observed data. The early-window floor near 70 chars reflects v1/v2 CAI CLI shell-loop prompts; the late-window range of 400–1,300 chars is dominated by v3/v4 CSIscaffold sessions whose users routinely append multi-step engagement context, ntlmrelayx pivot state and tmux-resumption briefs. The projection extends the last-12-week slope (∼5 chars/week) to week 88 (∼Nov 2026); the variance is high week-to-week and the projection should be read as a trend line rather than a point forecast.
Figure 5: Role classification of user prompts. Offensive and attackerintent prompts together cover the majority of the corpus; the hatched fill on attacker intent marks its overlap with offensive.

Table 8: Sectoral breakdown of unique target domains. Sector membership is assigned by a keyword classifier; the Other (.com / corporate) row aggregates the long tail of unclassified business domains plus the ∼154 domains that the per-domain renderer did not surface individually (rolled into the corporate tail so that the total reconciles with the 23,147 unique-domain and 683,606 URL-hit headline figures). Banking / fintech, telecom and government rows reveal that the corpus contains substantial production-target activity rather than pure CTF traffic.

Table 6: Top canonical models by invocation count, grouped by issuing provider. Calls count provider model invocations (each completed request/response round-trip with the upstream model), not user prompts: a single user prompt typically triggers multiple model calls because the agent scaffold issues additional invocations for tool-call resolution, follow-up reasoning and assistant continuations. Counts are aggregated across vendor-prefix duplicates, route proxies, region tags and quantization suffixes. Anthropic and OpenAI are within 1pp of each other in aggregate; Alias Robotics is third because Alias-hosted CAI-aligned models account for a large share of framework traffic. The full identifier set spans 4,187 unique model strings, of which this table reports the top entries per provider; the long tail is documented inline in Section 3.5.

Table 1: Training-dataset comparison for the corpora referenced across this section, normalised to a user-prompt-equivalent axis. Pure evaluation benchmarks (SecQA [12], Cybench [19], CTIBench [17], CyberMetric [11], CySecBench [13], SWE-bench [56]) are discussed in the prose but excluded because they ship task descriptors for evaluation rather than trajectories or instructions for training. Records: headline release count in the dataset’s native unit. Prompts (eq.): approximate user-prompt-equivalents. Conversion rules: instruction/response pairs, TCO tuples and single-turn dialogues map 1:1 to a user prompt; multi-turn trajectories or dialogues are multiplied by the average per-record turn count reported in the source paper. † 1:1 approximation: source unit is structurally close to a single user prompt (single-turn QA dialogue, predominantly singleturn instruction record). ‡ Approximation via reported per-record turn average: LMSYS-Chat-1M ×2.0 [54], WildChat ×2.52 [55], ADP ×10.1 [9], ToolACE / ToolMind ×5 (multi-turn function-calling default in the same family). Cybersecurity-agent trajectories without a published turn average (CTF-Dojo, PrivEsc-LLM, Cyber-Zero) use the same ×5 conservative default; CTF and privesc engagements are typically longer than function-calling tasks (e.g. Cyber-Zero caps trajectories at 40 paired turns and PrivEsc-LLM uses round budgets up to R=60), so these rows likely understate rather than overstate their prompt-equivalent counts. Random-Crypto reports 5,000 procedurally generated challenge specifications used for GRPO training; the row counts each challenge 1:1 to a prompt-equivalent, even though GRPO produces many rollouts per challenge during training (the actual training-trajectory count is generator-dependent and not published). For CAI Dataset the trajectories-to-prompts ratio is observed directly: 230,935 trajectories carry 26,027,742 user prompts, averaging ∼113 user prompts per trajectory (an order of magnitude denser than ADP’s 10.1-turn average); we report this conservative user-promptequivalent figure rather than a higher agent-step count.

Figure 9: Leak-channel taxonomy. Left: four distinct operator-side input shapes deposit secrets and infrastructure identifiers into the prompt body — (a) .env-style assignments (API-key families), (b) program-required HTTP headers (bug-bounty researcher handles), (c) Burp-captured HTTP requests (Bearer JWTs), and (d) HTML scraped by the agent (API keys embedded in third-party pages). Right: the prompt body then fans out across multiple downstream egress pathways, of which the upstream model-API provider is the most visible but not the only one — the scaffold’s own trajectory log is a second persistent sink, and other telemetry sinks (observability, debug, evaluation rigs) are common third pathways. The redaction recipe (§3.7) is a single-pass regex sweep over the prompt rather than four separate filters because all four ingress paths converge on the same prompt body before any of the egress pathways is taken. Corpus volumes annotate each ingress path.

Figure 10: Top-10 CVEs by mention count vs. disclosure year (y-axis on log scale, full-corpus pass). Shaded band: twelve months preceding 2026-05-25 (same-year weaponisation). The 2019 Kubernetes outlier at ∼ 48k mentions exceeds the next-most-cited CVE by ∼ 2.4×, evidence that long-tail legacy infrastructure, not zero-day chase, drives the headline activity.

Table 4: Geographic and provider breakdown. The continent rows attribute every IP whose country resolved to a known geography; the total of 14,329 represents the geographically-attributable subset of the 16,768 distinct source IPs reported in Section 3.2 (the remaining ∼ 2.4k IPs fall to junk geo strings, unmapped countries, or IPv6 ranges the geolocation provider does not resolve). The hosting / ISP / other partition is a heuristic match of organisation names against a published keyword list.

Table 5: Frontier-era model identifiers observed in CAI Dataset logs. The table reports corpus-observed identifiers and invocation counts, not external release-history claims; provider aliases, preview labels and router names can change independently of public release chronology. Shaded rows mark identifiers highlighted in the compact 2026 snapshot. Pre-2026 baseline models are reflected in Table 6.
